edges.title: Couperin’s Parnassus apotheosis of Corelli

works.to: Le Parnasse, ou L’Apothéose de Corelli (1724)

edges.claim: Couperin’s trio sonata of 1724 depicts Corelli’s ascent of Parnassus in seven named movements. In them Corelli petitions the Muses, drinks at Hippocrene, sleeps, and takes his place beside Apollo.

works.to: L’Apothéose de Lully (1725)

edges.claim: In Couperin’s 1725 instrumental homage, Apollo persuades Lully and Corelli to unite French and Italian tastes. According to the movement headings, Lully plays the subject while Corelli accompanies, and then they swap.

edges.claim: Vivaldi ended his first published collection of trio sonatas with variations on La Folia for two violins and continuo. The opening Adagio states the inherited melody in D minor. In the variations the tempo changes and the violins play in fast running figures.

edges.title: Bach’s overextended leave in Lübeck

works.to: Bach’s visit of 1705–06

edges.claim: Bach obtained leave from his Arnstadt post in 1705 to visit Lübeck and hear Buxtehude, but remained away into 1706. Called before the consistory on his return, he explained that he had travelled to learn things connected with his art.

edges.title: Frescobaldi’s organ Masses and Bach

works.to: Bach’s study copy of Fiori musicali

edges.claim: A manuscript of Frescobaldi’s Fiori musicali bore Bach’s name and the date 1714. It contained chant-based Kyrie versets, canzonas and ricercars, Italian liturgical organ music that Bach had in his own copy. The volume was lost during the Second World War.
edges.note: Older accounts call this Bach’s complete autograph copy. The 2026 source suggests a scribal copy signed and dated by him. The copyist’s identity remains uncertain; the edge records manuscript transmission.

edges.title: Bach’s copy of a French organ book

works.to: Bach’s copy of Grigny’s organ collection

edges.claim: Bach’s autograph copy of Grigny’s Premier livre d’orgue survives in Frankfurt as Mus Hs 1538. In the same manuscript he also copied Dieupart’s harpsichord suites and d’Anglebert’s ornament table, so French repertory and instructions for playing its ornaments entered his working library together.
edges.note: The holding library dates the composite manuscript 1709–14, with catalogue metadata c. 1710. The timeline follows that approximate catalogue date.

edges.claim: Bach’s A-minor keyboard Sonata BWV 965 is an arrangement of Reincken’s first sonata from Hortus musicus, an ensemble work, for a single keyboard player. He kept its succession of introductory, fugal and dance movements.

edges.title: Music for two solo violins on Bach’s organ

works.from: Concerto in A minor, Op. 3 No. 8, RV 522 (1711)
works.to: Organ Concerto in A minor, BWV 593 (c. 1713)

edges.claim: Bach transcribed Vivaldi’s A-minor concerto for two violins, strings and continuo as the solo-organ Concerto BWV 593 around 1713. He used the two manuals to separate tutti and solo material, and he added ornaments, detail in the middle voices and fuller chords while keeping the structure of the concerto.
edges.note: The transcription is documented. The date of c. 1713 is approximate, and it is probable, though not certain, that Prince Johann Ernst supplied the print.

edges.title: Four violins arranged for four harpsichords

works.from: Concerto in B minor, Op. 3 No. 10, RV 580
works.to: Concerto for four harpsichords in A minor, BWV 1065 (c. 1730)

edges.claim: Bach arranged Vivaldi’s B-minor concerto for four violins as an A-minor concerto for four harpsichords and strings. Each violin line becomes a keyboard part for two hands. The slow movement, built on broken chords, stays especially close to Vivaldi’s original.
edges.note: Around 1730 is an estimate. The original performers are unknown; Bach and three of his children have been proposed.

edges.title: Oboe concerto arranged as keyboard ornament study

works.from: Oboe Concerto in D minor, S D935
works.to: Keyboard Concerto in D minor, BWV 974 (c. 1713–14)

edges.claim: Bach made BWV 974 from Alessandro Marcello’s D-minor oboe concerto. In the arrangement one keyboard plays the oboe and string parts, and Bach wrote out more elaborate ornaments for the solo line.
edges.note: The transcription is dated approximately 1713–14; the route by which the manuscript reached Weimar is uncertain.

edges.title: Stabat mater reworked as a German psalm

works.to: Tilge, Höchster, meine Sünden, BWV 1083 (1740s)

edges.claim: Bach fitted a German paraphrase of Psalm 51 to Pergolesi’s Stabat mater. The music of the Latin Marian lament became Tilge, Höchster, meine Sünden, BWV 1083, a German penitential psalm.
edges.note: 1746 falls within the source’s alternative dating ranges of 1744–48 and 1745–47. The exact first-performance date is unknown.

edges.title: Contrapuntal setting of Luther’s hymn

works.from: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott
works.to: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott, BWV 80, Leipzig versions

edges.claim: Bach expanded an earlier Weimar cantata into a Leipzig Reformation cantata on Luther’s Ein feste Burg. In the opening movement the instruments play the chorale in long notes while the chorus sings in imitation around it.
edges.note: The Leipzig work developed in stages; 1730 is an approximate date. The later trumpet parts were added by Wilhelm Friedemann Bach.

edges.title: Credo intonation in Bach’s counterpoint

works.from: Plainchant intonation, Credo in unum Deum
works.to: Mass in B minor, BWV 232, opening Credo

edges.claim: Bach based the opening of the B-minor Mass’s Credo on an older chant intonation for the words Credo in unum Deum. He set the borrowed head-motif in measured rhythm over a walking continuo bass.
edges.note: 1749 is the approximate date by which the Mass was assembled; when the movement was first conceived is harder to date. The year 800 given for the tradition node places chant broadly on the timeline.

edges.title: Couperin in the Bach family notebook

works.from: Les Bergeries, Second livre, Sixième ordre (1717)
works.to: Anna Magdalena Bach’s 1725 notebook, No. 6, BWV Anh. 183

edges.claim: Couperin’s Les Bergeries was published in 1717 and was known in the Bach household. The B♭-major rondeau appears as No. 6 in Anna Magdalena’s 1725 notebook.
edges.note: The year is that of the notebook, to which entries were added over time. The edge records a household copy; the entry has not been authenticated as being in Johann Sebastian’s hand.

edges.title: Zachow: counterpoint and foreign repertory

works.to: Handel’s childhood training

edges.claim: Before his Hamburg apprenticeship, Handel studied with the Halle organist Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow. As well as counterpoint and figured bass, Zachow taught his pupil Italian and French instrumental music.
edges.note: 1693 is an approximate date for the childhood timeline. The cited scholarly account explicitly qualifies details inherited from Mainwaring’s retrospective biography.

edges.title: Alternation of Milton’s opposed poems in Handel’s ode

works.to: L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato (1740)

edges.claim: Charles Jennens interleaved passages from Milton’s companion poems for Handel’s L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato, first performed in London on 27 February 1740. The third part, Il Moderato, is Jennens’s own.

edges.title: Dryden’s musical feast at Covent Garden

works.from: Alexander’s Feast, or the Power of Musick
works.to: Alexander’s Feast, HWV 75 (1736)

edges.claim: The Covent Garden advertisement for 19 February 1736 announced a new ode written by the late Dryden and set by Handel. A letter of 24 January records that, while the work was in preparation, Handel played nearly all of it to Shaftesbury, who singled out the chorus beginning ‘Happy, happy’.

edges.title: Roman keyboard contest, as anecdote

works.to: Scarlatti’s reported encounter with Handel

edges.claim: In the story handed down by Handel’s biographer Mainwaring, Handel and Scarlatti competed at Cardinal Ottoboni’s in Rome. Handel won on the organ.
edges.note: The contest’s exact date, judging and details lack contemporary confirmation in the sources consulted. Sandra Dolby traces the second-hand, oral transmission of Mainwaring’s Italian anecdotes. The year 1708 follows the cited concise biography.

edges.title: Emanuel’s only music teacher

works.to: C. P. E. Bach’s training in keyboard and composition

edges.claim: In the autobiography prepared for Burney and published in 1773, Emanuel Bach named his father as his only teacher of composition and keyboard playing. He listed his own first published keyboard minuet under 1731.
edges.note: The timeline uses Emanuel’s first listed publication in 1731 to locate his early training. The full span of his lessons is uncertain.

works.from: C. P. E. Bach’s keyboard sonatas
works.to: Haydn’s independent keyboard studies

edges.claim: During his early years of independent study, Haydn returned repeatedly to Emanuel Bach’s keyboard sonatas. He later recalled playing them over and over.

works.to: Gradus ad Parnassum (1725)

edges.claim: Fux’s Gradus ad Parnassum is set out as an imaginary counterpoint lesson. Aloysius stands for Palestrina, Josephus for Fux. Haydn and Beethoven later worked through the lessons on paper.

works.to: Haydn’s self-directed counterpoint exercises

edges.claim: According to Griesinger, Haydn worked the counterpoint exercises in Fux’s treatise, put them aside, and later went back to check them. He kept a worn copy of the treatise.

edges.claim: In Vienna, Haydn accompanied pupils in Porpora’s singing lessons and received instruction in return. Porpora’s teaching connected composition with singing and Italian declamation, alongside the keyboard and counterpoint that Haydn studied on his own.
edges.note: 1753 is an approximate placement within the early-1750s association; the sources give slightly different ranges for Porpora’s Vienna residence.

works.to: Haydn’s London experience in 1791

edges.claim: On his first London visit, Haydn attended the Handel commemoration at the end of May 1791. There he heard Handel’s choral music performed on a festival scale, years before he wrote his own English-inspired oratorios.

works.to: Three keyboard concertos, K. 107 (after 1770)

edges.claim: Mozart’s three concertos K. 107 are arrangements of Johann Christian Bach’s Op. 5 Nos. 2, 3 and 4 as works for keyboard with strings. The surviving manuscript is in the hands of both Wolfgang and Leopold, so the arrangements record the two working together on concerto writing, as well as Wolfgang’s admiration for the London Bach.
edges.note: 1771 is approximate. The NMA dates the manuscript no earlier than the end of 1770 and probably later.

edges.title: Spanish guitar strumming in the keyboard sonata

works.to: Keyboard Sonata in A minor, K. 175

edges.claim: Scarlatti’s Sonata in A minor, K. 175, is built on dense, dissonant chords played with the attack of a guitarist. Giulio d’Amore hears Andalusian strumming and dance in the piece.
edges.note: The Andalusian connection is d’Amore’s stylistic interpretation; no specific folk melody or commission has been identified. The year 1752 is the date of the principal Venice manuscript copy; the date of composition is uncertain. The year 1700 given for the tradition node is an approximate display date.

edges.title: The nymph’s lament over a descending fourth

works.from: The descending minor tetrachord as a ground
works.to: Lamento della ninfa, SV 163, published in Madrigals Book VIII (1638)

edges.claim: In Monteverdi’s Lamento della ninfa, the abandoned nymph sings over a bass that falls through four notes and then starts again. The piece appeared in his eighth book of madrigals in 1638.
edges.note: The edge identifies the shared descending-bass convention. The tradition node’s year 1600 is an approximate historical display date.

edges.title: Descending ground for solo violin

works.to: Passacaglia in G minor, C. 105, concluding the Mystery Sonatas (c. 1676)

edges.claim: Biber’s Passacaglia for unaccompanied violin repeats the descending figure G–F–E♭–D, from tonic down to dominant, throughout. The four notes are heard on their own, within chords or inside quick figuration, and the single violin plays both the ground and its variations.
edges.note: The date is approximate. The manuscript’s guardian-angel image supports a consoling reading of the descending tetrachord, as the cited programme explains.

edges.title: Dido’s farewell over a chromatic descent

works.from: The chromatic descending fourth and ground-bass convention
works.to: When I am laid in earth, Dido and Aeneas, Z. 626

edges.claim: In Purcell’s When I am laid in earth, the bass descends chromatically through G minor and then repeats from the beginning. Above it, Dido asks again and again to be remembered.
edges.note: An early Chelsea performance dates from 1689; composition and première dates are uncertain. The bass follows an inherited convention; how it reached Purcell is unknown.

edges.title: Bach: chromatic descent in a chorus of tears

works.to: Weinen, Klagen, Sorgen, Zagen, BWV 12, opening chorus (1714)

edges.claim: The opening chorus of Bach’s BWV 12 sets the voices over a repeating chromatic descending bass. First performed in Weimar on 22 April 1714, it moves to a contrasting middle section and returns to the same ground; Bach later reworked it as the Crucifixus of the B-minor Mass.

edges.title: Return of the lament ground at the Crucifixion

works.from: The chromatic ground of BWV 12 and the lament-bass convention
works.to: Mass in B minor, BWV 232, Crucifixus (assembled c. 1748–49)

edges.claim: For the Crucifixus, Bach reworked the lamenting chorus of BWV 12 in E minor. The bass repeats beneath the words of the Crucifixion and burial, then modulates near the end to G major before the Resurrection movement.
edges.note: Bach’s reuse of BWV 12 is documented. The Bethlehem commentary also compares Purcell’s bass; no direct connection between the two composers’ grounds has been proven.

edges.title: Thirty-two variations on a falling bass

works.to: Thirty-two Variations in C minor, WoO 80, theme (1806)

edges.claim: Beethoven’s C-minor Variations, WoO 80, begin with a chromatically descending bass. He kept to its short harmonic scheme through thirty-two variations for piano.
edges.note: The edge identifies the bass pattern. No specific earlier source has been documented, and there is no record that Beethoven assigned it a lament programme.

works.to: Couplets de folies, Pièces de viole, Livre II, No. 20 (1701)

edges.claim: Marais included Couplets de folies in his second book of viol pieces in 1701: a theme and thirty-one variations for bass viol and continuo. The same D-minor framework was also used by Corelli for violin and by Vivaldi in a trio sonata.
